one_line: Write full sentences and give each point its reason or detail. Answer the question on the paper, using its scenario.

points.heading: Write in full sentences
points.text: No Cambridge document for 9626 asks for bullet points. The Cambridge Learner Guide has a section of advice for all of Papers 1 and 3. Its first line tells you to answer in sentences.

cites.quote: Advice for all Papers 1 and 3 Answer the questions in sentences. Never give ‘one word’ or one ‘phrase’ answers.

points.heading: Write in full sentences
points.text: Examiner reports give this advice in almost every exam series. Use full sentences for Describe and Explain answers as well as for the long questions.

cites.quote: Candidates should also be encouraged to write full sentences and discouraged from writing bulleted, short statements in their responses. Descriptions or explanations can only be conveyed in full sentences.

points.heading: Write in full sentences
points.text: Bullets usually leave out what earns the marks. A bullet is often a bare point, and most of the marks go to the reason or detail that should follow it.

cites.quote: Short statements or bulleted responses that do not expand on facts cannot be awarded the higher marks because these are not discussions.

points.heading: Lists and tables in long answers
points.text: Shape matters too in Discuss, Evaluate and Analyse answers. Bulleted lists and tables of statements cannot get most of the marks. Separate lists of benefits and drawbacks have the same problem when each item is one word or a very short sentence.

cites.quote: learners who produced bulleted lists or tables of statements were unable to access most of the marks
This comment also applies to answers that have separate lists of benefits and drawbacks, but the lists consist of single word or very brief sentences.

points.heading: Lists and tables in long answers
points.text: The mark schemes once printed this rule too. From 2021 to 2023, almost every Paper 1 and Paper 3 mark scheme limited bulleted answers to Discuss, Evaluate or Analyse questions. On an 8-mark question, the limit was 6 marks, however good the points were. Shorter questions had lower limits, for example 3 of 4 marks.

cites.quote: Max. six marks if bullets/list of points Must have expansions or comparisons to be a proper discussion
three marks if bullets/list of points

points.heading: Lists and tables in long answers
points.text: In 2024, only the March and June Paper 3 mark schemes still printed the limit. From November 2024, the mark schemes leave it out. The 2025 examiner reports still say that bulleted lists and tables cannot get most of the marks.

cites.quote: Max 6 marks if bullets/list of points.
learners who produced bulleted lists or tables of statements were unable to access most of the marks

points.heading: Lists and tables in long answers
points.text: One Paper 1 question in November 2025 asked for the steps of planning something. The examiners accepted a list of steps, sometimes bulleted, or a description. Each step had to show a decision. Everywhere else, the examiner reports ask for full sentences.

cites.quote: In the first, candidates listed (sometimes by creating a bulleted list) steps that would be taken, whilst others described the steps that had been taken. Either method was acceptable

points.heading: Points and their detail
points.text: You do not lose marks for grammar or spelling. Examiners give marks for correct points and do not take marks away for errors. Your meaning must still be clear.

cites.quote: answers should only be judged on the quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar when these features are specifically assessed by the question as indicated by the mark scheme. The meaning, however, should be unambiguous.

points.heading: Points and their detail
points.text: Short sentences are fine. Put one clear point in each sentence. Each point is then easy for the examiner to mark and easy for you to check.

cites.quote: Keep most sentences short and focused. That will help with clarity and in making every point stand out for the examiner.

points.heading: Points and their detail
points.text: Some mark schemes give one mark for a point and a further mark only for its reason or detail. They label the first mark (1st), with the linked follow-on marks under it. Some mark schemes say that the follow-on marks need the first one. One examiner report says the further marks were 'dependant on this answer'. Cambridge's mark-scheme key does not define (1st).

cites.quote: (only award if either of previous two marks given)
Two further marks were then dependant on this answer.

points.heading: Points and their detail
points.text: One mark scheme limits an answer made only of bare points. On that 3-mark question, answers that are all first marks get at most 2 marks.

cites.quote: MAX two marks if answers are all only first marks.

points.heading: Answer the question on the paper
points.text: Answer the question that the paper asks. Only answers that use the scenario in the question can reach the full range of marks. Do not write everything you know about one word in the question.

cites.quote: the full range of marks is only available to candidates for answers referring to the scenario in the questions
Centres must ensure that candidates target their answers to the questions as they are written and not at ‘key’ words in the questions.

points.heading: Answer the question on the paper
points.text: Do not write out mark scheme bullets that you learnt by heart. Examiners notice this. A list of learnt points does not answer a new question.

cites.quote: Examiners saw many scripts where candidates listed sets of bullet points that appeared to have been learnt directly from previous mark schemes.

points.heading: Answer the question on the paper
points.text: Use the number of marks as a clue. It tells you how many separate points, or how much detail, the examiner expects to see in your answer.

cites.quote: the number of marks available for each question is a useful indicator of how much detail or how many descriptions should be given in the answers

points.heading: Answer the question on the paper
points.text: Never leave a question blank. A few sentences on a topic you are unsure of can still earn marks.

cites.quote: Writing a few sentences, even if little is known about the topic, may gain valuable marks towards the overall total.
